top_choice_rationale: P003 (Persson, Tabellini, Besley) credits a formal framework, with empirical tests, for how constitutions, electoral rules and state capacity shape fiscal policy. The core is about three decades old, so it has been replicated, extended and criticised. It has the most concentrated credit structure among the larger proposals. The 2024 prize concerned the origins of institutions, whereas this work takes institutions as given and asks what policies they produce. I treat that proximity as a timing question, not a scientific one. Its main weakness is cross-country identification with endogenous adoption, so the citation should claim a framework and its tests, not causal settlement. P001 is second because its designs are the most checkable, but its core results are under a decade old and the Katz seat is open. P002 (Kiyotaki-Moore) is third. It has the cleanest attribution and a mature mechanism, but marginal novelty relative to the 2022 prize and mostly indirect aggregate evidence count against it. P004 is fourth because a three-name cut of an eight-name field cannot be defended on a clear principle. Any award is preferred to no award.
recusal_note: Field adjacency to P003: my work on comparative political institutions, measurement of democracy and state-building is close to the political-economics literature. I gave the 2024 presentation speech on the institutions prize, which may colour my contrast with P003, and the speech may reflect collective drafting. My profile lists a co-author surnamed Persson (with Rothstein, on corruption as a collective-action problem) without a first name, and I have no basis to treat this as Torsten Persson. No listed co-authorship or institutional tie to Tabellini, Besley, Chetty, Hendren, Friedman, Kiyotaki, Moore, Calvo, Taylor or Woodford is apparent from the profile. Disclosure only, not adjudicated.
